message.content:
In lions, one of the most striking examples of a dominant genetic trait is the development of the mane in adult male lions. The presence of a mane is governed by a dominant allele (often referred to as **M**). When a male lion inherits at least one copy of this dominant allele from either parent, he will develop a mane. If he inherits two copies of the recessive allele (**m**), he will not develop a mane.

This dominant trait is also evident in coat color. The allele for a black coat color is dominant over the allele for a lighter or spotted coat. Thus, a lion that inherits at least one copy of the dominant black allele will display a black coat, while only lions homozygous for the recessive allele will show a lighter or spotted pattern.
